# Multi-Provider LLM Routing via Gateway APIs

A citation-backed analysis of LLM gateway platforms, routing patterns, and
the trade-offs of unified gateways versus direct provider integration.

## Executive Summary

LLM gateways have emerged as critical infrastructure for production AI
applications. They solve three problems simultaneously: provider resilience
(failover when providers go down), cost optimization (routing to cheaper
models when quality allows), and operational simplicity (one API, one bill,
one dashboard).

The gateway landscape in 2026 is maturing rapidly. LiteLLM (41.8k GitHub
stars [12]) and Portkey (~11.1k stars [11]) lead the open-source space.
OpenRouter is the dominant managed gateway with 300+ models and a
straightforward 5.5% credit fee [1][2]. Newer entrants like Bifrost achieve
11µs routing overhead [22], showing the performance ceiling is very low.

**Key finding:** Intelligent routing can reduce LLM costs by 35-85% while
maintaining 95% of frontier model performance [29]. RouteLLM (LMSYS)
demonstrated that only 14-26% of queries actually need GPT-4-class models —
the rest can be handled by cheaper alternatives [29].

**At moderate scale:** OpenRouter's 5.5% fee is reasonable for a system
that needs multi-model support without infrastructure overhead. At high volume
or when compliance controls are needed, migrating to self-hosted
LiteLLM is straightforward (same OpenAI-compatible API). The routing layer
is not the bottleneck — the choice between gateway and direct integration
matters less than having fallback chains and cost controls in place.

### OpenRouter Architecture

OpenRouter's routing uses a three-tier load balancing approach [5]:
1. **Stability filter** — prioritizes providers without outages in last 30s
2. **Price-weighted selection** — inverse-square weighting by cost (a provider
   at $1/M tokens gets 9× more traffic than one at $3/M tokens)
3. **Fallback chain** — remaining providers as backup

Developers can override defaults via a `provider` object: sort by
price/throughput/latency, whitelist/blacklist providers, set minimum throughput
thresholds, enforce cost ceilings, and require Zero Data Retention [5].
Shortcuts like `:nitro` (highest throughput) and `:floor` (lowest cost)
provide quick access to common routing preferences [5].

### Martian: Cautionary Note

Martian raised $9M and received Accenture investment [18][19], but its
website now positions the company as a research organization focused on model
understanding rather than a routing product [17]. This is worth noting when
evaluating the gateway landscape — not all entrants persist.

## 2. Gateway vs Direct Integration

### When to Use a Gateway

**Use a gateway when [20][21][26]:**
- Running multiple models across providers (40% of teams do this [73])
- Need failover — OpenAI and Anthropic both had 20+ incidents in Dec 2025 alone [40]
- Want consolidated billing and cost attribution per team/project [21]
- Need spending limits — a developer reported $247 overnight from a Make.com
  bug with direct API, no kill switch [20]

**Use direct API when [28]:**
- Small project with limited scope and risk
- 100% committed to a single provider
- Need bleeding-edge features immediately (gateways lag)
- Performance is critical and every millisecond matters

### Latency Reality

Purpose-built gateways add 2-20ms overhead [73]. Bifrost achieves 11µs [22].
For context, LLM inference itself takes 500ms-5s for most requests — gateway
overhead is noise. Self-hosting eliminates 100-400ms of network overhead vs
managed services.

### Vendor Lock-in

Migration costs average $315,000 per project [24] when lock-in has spread
into fine-tuning, conversation histories, and embeddings. Gateways mitigate
this: swapping providers is often a one-line base URL change with
OpenAI-compatible APIs [14][8][2].

Gartner predicts 70% of organizations building multi-LLM apps will use an AI
gateway by 2028, up from <5% in 2024 [26].

**Counter-risk:** The gateway itself can become a lock-in vector. Evaluate
"can you leave later" — self-hosted OSS gateways (LiteLLM, Portkey, Bifrost)
with standard APIs mitigate this [74].

### Enterprise Case Study: Uber

Uber built a centralized GenAI Gateway serving 60+ use cases [21]. Drivers:
PII redaction before sending to external LLMs, cost attribution per team,
and eliminating redundant integration efforts across departments. Supports
OpenAI, Vertex AI, and self-hosted models [21].

See [references/gateway-vs-direct.md](references/gateway-vs-direct.md) for
full analysis.

## 3. Routing Patterns

### Cost-Based Routing (Highest Impact)

The most impactful routing pattern is cost-based: route simple queries to
cheap models, complex ones to expensive models.

**RouteLLM (LMSYS, ICLR 2025) [29]:**
- 85% cost reduction on MT Bench at 95% GPT-4 performance
- Matrix factorization router: only 26% of queries need GPT-4 (48% cheaper
  than random routing)
- With data augmentation: only 14% GPT-4 calls needed (75% savings)
- Outperformed commercial alternatives (Martian, Unify AI) by 40%

**Real-world validation [33]:** Customer support platform cut monthly LLM
spend from $42,000 to $18,000 routing simple queries to Claude 3.5 Haiku
and complex escalations to Sonnet — same customer satisfaction scores.

### Cascading (Quality-Based)

Start with the cheapest model. If quality checks fail, escalate to the next
tier [70][34]:
1. Generate response with cheap model
2. Self-verify (consistency check or confidence score)
3. If insufficient, escalate to larger model

Cascading with reliable quality judges achieves 5× cost savings at negligible
performance degradation [34]. Hybrid approaches allow 40% fewer calls to large
models with no quality drop [35].

### Semantic Routing

Uses vector embeddings for routing decisions instead of LLM classification [31].
Reduces routing latency from ~5000ms (LLM-based) to ~100ms (vector math) [31].
Combined with semantic caching: 40-70% cost reduction, 7× latency
improvement [48].

### Fallback Chains

Sequential provider attempts when primary fails [45][15]:
- 429 Too Many Requests → reroute immediately
- 500/502/503/529 → retry with backoff, then fallback
- Do NOT trigger fallback on 400/401 (client errors) [45]

**Critical constraint [41]:** Once streaming tokens to a user, you cannot
retry with a different model. Fallback only works before first token.

See [references/routing-patterns.md](references/routing-patterns.md) for all
seven patterns analyzed.

## 4. Failover and Resilience

### Provider Reliability (December 2025) [40]

| Provider | Incidents | Major | Avg Resolution |
|----------|-----------|-------|----------------|
| OpenAI | 22 | 1 | 498 min |
| Anthropic | 20 | 7 | 553 min |
| Google Gemini | 0 | 0 | N/A |

Both OpenAI and Anthropic had ~183 hours of total incident time in December
2025 alone [40]. Outages happen 1-2 times per quarter [42]. LLM providers
are not reliable enough for single-provider production deployments.

### Production Resilience: Assembled Case Study [41]

- **<0.001% request failure rate** during multi-hour provider outage
- **Failover in hundreds of milliseconds** (down from 5+ min manual switchover)
- **99.97% effective uptime** despite multiple provider outages
- Trade-off: 20-30% increase in evaluation burden (every prompt change
  must be tested against fallback providers)

### Circuit Breaker Configuration [43][42]

Typical production settings:
- 5 consecutive failures or >5% error rate → circuit opens
- 30-60 second recovery timeout
- 3 consecutive successes → circuit closes
- Salesforce: 40%+ failures in 60s window → bypass retries, route to Azure
  OpenAI; reset after 20 minutes [42]

See [references/failover-resilience.md](references/failover-resilience.md)
for detailed patterns.

## 5. Security Analysis

### Compliance Landscape

| Gateway | SOC 2 | ISO 27001 | GDPR | HIPAA |
|---------|-------|-----------|------|-------|
| Portkey | Type 2 (Enterprise) [10] | Yes [10] | Yes [10] | Enterprise [10] |
| LiteLLM | Type I + II [13] | Yes [13] | Via infra [13] | Via enterprise |
| OpenRouter | Not disclosed [7] | Not disclosed [7] | EU endpoint [4] | Not disclosed |

### Critical Security Concern: Supply Chain

LiteLLM experienced a supply chain attack on March 24, 2026 [16]. Versions
1.82.7/1.82.8 were compromised for ~40 minutes with a credential stealer
targeting environment variables, SSH keys, and cloud credentials [16][50].
The attack originated from a compromised CI/CD dependency [50].

**Implication:** Self-hosted gateways eliminate third-party data interception
but introduce supply chain risk. Pin dependencies and use verified Docker
images.

### Data Handling

OpenRouter does not log by default — it routes to providers with their own
policies [4]. Zero Data Retention (ZDR) prevents storage beyond in-memory
processing [53]. EU endpoint (eu.openrouter.ai) keeps data within the EU [4].

LiteLLM Cloud tracks usage data but "does not access or store the message/
response content of your API requests or responses" [13]. Self-hosted:
zero data transmitted to LiteLLM servers [13].

See [references/security-compliance.md](references/security-compliance.md)
for full analysis.

## 6. Cost Analysis

### Gateway Cost Comparison

| Gateway | Fee Structure | At $100/mo LLM spend |
|---------|--------------|---------------------|
| OpenRouter | 5.5% credit fee [2] | $5.50 |
| Portkey Production | $49/mo flat [9] | $49.00 |
| LiteLLM (self-hosted) | Infrastructure + DevOps [27] | $2,280–$2,680/mo |
| Bifrost (self-hosted) | Infrastructure only [63] | Varies |
| Direct API | $0 gateway cost | $0 (but no failover) |

**Break-even [27]:** Self-hosting becomes cost-effective above 40-100M
tokens/month. Below 20M tokens/month, managed services win when factoring
DevOps time.

### Optimization Strategies (Stackable)

1. **Intelligent routing:** 35-85% savings [29][70]
2. **Semantic caching:** 40-70% additional savings on cache hits [48]
3. **Model downsizing:** Only 14-26% of queries need frontier models [29]
4. **Spending limits:** Prevent runaway costs from bugs [20]

See [references/cost-modeling.md](references/cost-modeling.md) for detailed
analysis.

## 7. Open-Source Gateway Ecosystem

The OSS ecosystem is active and competitive. For self-hosted routing:

- **LiteLLM** — broadest provider support, largest community, but Python
  performance limits and a recent supply chain incident [12][16]
- **Portkey Gateway** — lightest footprint (<1ms, 122kb), TypeScript [11]
- **Bifrost** — fastest (11µs), Go-based, Apache 2.0, but newest [22][63]
- **Kong AI Gateway** — best for teams already using Kong for APIs [56]

**vLLM** (75k stars [54]) is primarily an inference server but released
Semantic Router v0.1 (Iris) in early 2026 with intelligent routing
capabilities [32]. **TGI** from Hugging Face is a model serving solution,
not a multi-provider gateway [55].

See [references/open-source-routing.md](references/open-source-routing.md)
for comprehensive comparison.

## 8. Practical Recommendations

For an architecture using OpenRouter as unified gateway with routing
to Claude/GPT-4/Gemini/Llama by invocation type:

### Keep OpenRouter (Current Scale)

OpenRouter is a reasonable choice at current scale. The 5.5% fee is justified
by [2][5][20]:
- Multi-model access without managing multiple API keys
- Automatic failover with inverse-square price-weighted load balancing
- Per-key spending limits preventing runaway costs
- Zero Data Retention option

### Add Resilience (Low Effort)

1. **Fallback chains in the orchestrator** — if OpenRouter itself goes
   down (46+ outages/year [6]), fall back to direct provider APIs for
   critical models
2. **Spending limits** — set per-key daily limits on OpenRouter [20]
3. **Monitor provider health** — track error rates and latency per model

### Consider Migration (If Scaling)

At high volume or needs compliance controls:
- **LiteLLM** — same OpenAI-compatible API, self-hosted, broadest provider
  support. Pin to verified Docker images given the March 2026 incident [16].
- **Portkey** — if observability and enterprise features matter more than
  community size

### Implement Cost-Based Routing

The highest-ROI improvement is cost-based routing within the orchestrator layer:
- Route simple tasks (summarization, classification) to cheaper models
- Reserve frontier models for complex reasoning
- RouteLLM showed 75% savings with 95% quality retention [29]

## 9. Limitations

### Source Quality

- Most performance benchmarks are vendor-published, not independently verified
- OpenRouter's trust center did not render extractable content [7]
- Kong's benchmark claiming 800%+ faster than LiteLLM [71] could not be
  verified (timeout) and is vendor-published
- Provider pricing is point-in-time; verify against current pricing pages

### Coverage Gaps

- Provider arbitrage (same model priced differently across providers) was
  identified but specific differentials were not verified via WebFetch
- Streaming-specific latency benchmarks are scarce
- Multi-turn conversation routing is under-researched
- Martian's current product status is unclear [17]

- 79 citations from web sources visited in-session

- Two verification sub-agents (citation audit + consistency review) run
  against all files
- Sources span official documentation (Tier 1), established tech company
